title: House Robber II (Circular Street)
statement: Houses are arranged in a circle, and nums[i] is the money in house i. Robbing two adjacent houses triggers the alarm, and because the street is a circle the first and last houses are adjacent too. Return the most money you can rob without ever taking two neighbours.
realWorld: Selecting non-conflicting items from a cyclic schedule: picking the most valuable shifts from a rotating weekly roster where Sunday night touches Monday morning, or choosing non-adjacent slots on a ring buffer of advertising positions. The circle is what makes it more than the straight-line version.

bruteForce.whySlow: 2^n subsets, of which only a Fibonacci-sized fraction are even legal — for n = 40 that is a trillion masks to build and throw away. The deeper waste is that the enumeration keeps re-deciding the same thing: the best plan for houses 5..n depends on one bit of history, namely whether house 4 was taken, yet every one of the exponentially many decisions about houses 0..4 causes the entire suffix to be re-explored from scratch.

patternIdentification: A constraint that ties the two ends of a sequence to each other. A left-to-right recurrence cannot express 'the first and last are neighbours', because when it reaches the last house it no longer remembers what it did at the first. The transferable move is: when a constraint couples the two ends, fix one end's decision and solve the rest linearly. Here the coupling forbids exactly one thing — taking both ends — so it is enough to solve two ordinary straight-line problems, one over houses 0..n-2 (the last is off the table) and one over houses 1..n-1 (the first is off the table), and take the better. The same trick unlocks circular subarrays, circular buffers and ring scheduling: enumerate the handful of cases the wrap-around creates, then reuse the linear solution unchanged.

optimized.idea: Solve the linear problem twice with one end removed each time. For the linear helper the state is dp[i] = the most money obtainable from the houses considered so far, ending at or before house i. The recurrence is dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]): either skip house i and keep the best so far, or take it and forfeit its neighbour. The base cases are dp = 0 before the range starts. Only the previous two values are ever read, so two ints replace the array.

commonMistakes: Running the plain linear solution once over the whole array and patching the result when both ends were taken. The fix is not local — dropping one end can change the optimal plan for the entire middle, not just remove one house. On [2,3,2] the unpatched linear answer is 4 (2 + 2) where the correct answer is 3.

Forgetting the single-house case. With n = 1 the two ranges become [0, -1] and [1, 0], both empty, so the loops never run and the function returns 0 instead of nums[0] — a silent zero on the smallest possible input.

Letting the circular neighbour rule apply when there is only one house — `next = (i + 1) % 1` is the house itself, so it appears to be adjacent to itself and rob([9]) returns 0 instead of 9. Any wrap-around adjacency needs the n == 1 case carved out.
